response:
Diagnosis after four evaluated generations: the alpha is concentrated in one channel and I can now name it precisely. Valuation legs built on *unencumbered liquid claims* — net cash to price, net current assets less all liabilities to price — earn positive FF5 alpha (+2.2% to +3.7%, t = 2.5–2.9) when paired with an operating-quality screen, while every conventional equity yield (GP/P, B/P, E/P, sales/P) earns high Fama-MacBeth t-stats and zero-to-negative alpha because HML and RMW already own it. Three further lessons: asset liquidity works as a *level* (act/at, +1.9%) but not as turnover (revt/act, −2.5%), so the mechanism is realisability rather than efficiency; accrual conservatism adds nothing to the liquid-claim leg (+0.3%, t=0.27); and the hidden-asset/depreciation story is dead (−2.0%). The best joint performer is net liquid claim × gross profitability (fmb 3.77, alpha +2.2%, t 2.55, coverage 0.121). This generation consolidates on that construct along four economically distinct margins — earnings capacity in the claim, obligation-scaled profitability, distributability of the claim, and through-cycle durability of the claim — plus one decomposition test and one short-side extension.

---SIGNAL 1---
NAME: Liquid Claim Plus Earning Power Cheapness
EXPRESSION: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(SUB(act, lt), MA(ADD(ib, dp), 3)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 3)))
HYPOTHESIS: A shareholder's claim has two parts — the liquid assets left after every obligation is met, and the durable cash the business generates each year — and a market price low relative to their sum, in a firm that also earns gross profit, is the sharpest available separation of quality value from distress.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: The archive's two largest alphas come from exactly these two ingredients used separately: the obligation-netted claim plus averaged cash earnings (+3.8%, t=3.2, but a negative cross-sectional slope) and the net liquid claim screened on gross profit (+2.2% with a 3.8 slope). Uniting the stock and flow components in the valuation leg while retaining the profitability rank tests whether the slope failure of the former was caused purely by the absence of a quality screen.
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional

---SIGNAL 2---
NAME: Liquid Claim With Obligation-Scaled Profit
EXPRESSION: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), lt), 3)))
HYPOTHESIS: The relevant measure of profitability for a discounted firm is not profit per dollar of assets but profit per dollar of obligation, because that is what determines whether the firm can outrun its creditors long enough for the discount to close.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: The archive's highest alpha used cash flow scaled by total liabilities as the quality leg but paid for it with coverage of 0.091, while the asset-scaled profitability version has full coverage but lower alpha; scaling gross profit by liabilities keeps the obligation-relative economics with near-universal coverage. Comparing it against the archived asset-scaled version on the same valuation leg isolates the scaling choice as the design question.
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional

---SIGNAL 3---
NAME: Liquid Claim That Is Actually Distributed
EXPRESSION: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(dvc, at)))
HYPOTHESIS: Liquid assets are only worth their carrying value to outside shareholders if management is willing to let cash leave the firm; a cheap, liquid balance sheet accompanied by real distributions is a verified claim, while the same balance sheet with no payout is an agency problem that the market discounts for good reason.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: Every positive-alpha signal in the archive rewards liquid claims, but none tests whether those claims are accessible, which is the standard free-cash-flow agency objection to cash-rich value; payout intensity is the observable that resolves it. Dividends are used as a verification channel on an already-validated valuation leg rather than as a standalone yield, so this is not a restatement of the dividend-yield anomaly, and industry ranking keeps the comparison within payout-similar peer groups.
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional

---SIGNAL 4---
NAME: Rich Price Funding Illiquid Asset Build
EXPRESSION: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), IND_RANK(GROWTH(SUB(at, act), 1)))
HYPOTHESIS: The worst corner of the valuation-quality space is a firm whose market price is high relative to a negative net liquid claim and which is simultaneously converting borrowed money into long-lived, hard-to-reverse assets; such firms have neither a liquid floor nor the option to stop, and should underperform.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: The archive's short-side attempts produced correct-signed alphas but the sign of the cross-sectional slope kept flipping because the valuation leg was a high book-to-market variant; orienting both legs toward the overpriced, illiquid, expanding corner aligns the two statistics. Growth in illiquid assets is a new quality channel here, distinct from the level-based strain ratio already tested, and speaks to irreversibility rather than to current leverage.
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional

---SIGNAL 5---
NAME: Liquid Assets To Price With Light Obligations
EXPRESSION: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(act, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(lt, at))))
HYPOTHESIS: Two separate things make a discount trustworthy — the firm owns realisable assets relative to its price, and it owes little relative to what it owns — and separating them identifies whether the return premium comes from having liquid resources or from lacking claims against them.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: All the winning valuation legs net obligations directly against liquid assets, which mechanically confounds the two effects and cancels them for firms where both are large; decomposing into a gross liquid-assets-to-price rank and a separate liability-intensity rank tells us which component the alpha comes from. Both legs have universal coverage and the multiplicative form places the long leg unambiguously at asset-rich, obligation-light firms.
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional

---SIGNAL 6---
NAME: Liquid Claim Tested Through The Cycle
EXPRESSION: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(TS_MIN(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), at), 5)))
HYPOTHESIS: A liquid balance sheet is a quality attribute only if it survived the firm's own bad years; a cheap firm whose net liquid position never fell far in five years has demonstrated structural solvency, while one whose current liquidity is a recent, cyclical high is a trap waiting for the next downturn.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: This makes the quality leg the worst-case value of the same balance-sheet state over five years, a through-cycle durability concept that no archived signal has tested and that FF5 cannot represent, while keeping the valuation leg that has produced the best joint evidence. It also repairs the failure mode of the earlier persistence-count design, whose zero counts destroyed the valuation ordering for a large mass of firms, because TS_MIN is continuous and defined for every firm with five years of data.
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional

---CRITIQUE Liquid Claim Plus Earning Power Cheapness---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 3
RATIONALE: The valuation leg adds an annual flow (3-yr average cash earnings) to a balance-sheet stock (act − lt) with an arbitrary implicit capitalization weight of 1x, and since the stock term is typically an order of magnitude larger and drives the cross-sectional dispersion, the signal is likely a near-duplicate of the archived "Net Liquid Claim Cheapness With Gross Profit" (identical quality leg, fmb 3.77 / alpha 2.2%) rather than a genuine test of whether the quality screen repaired the obligation-netted slope.

---CRITIQUE Liquid Claim With Obligation-Scaled Profit---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 2
RATIONALE: This is a denominator swap (at → lt) on the quality leg of an already-archived signal, and worse, it re-introduces 1/lt into a signal whose valuation leg already nets lt, so the two legs become mechanically correlated and the "profit per dollar of obligation" leg largely proxies low leverage — a screen the archive has tested repeatedly.

---CRITIQUE Liquid Claim That Is Actually Distributed---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 4
RATIONALE: Payout as verification that a liquid balance sheet is actually accessible to outside shareholders is a genuine free-cash-flow agency channel untested in the archive and not merely a restatement of dividend yield, though the reviewer should watch for a large tied mass of zero-dividend firms compressing the quality leg and for confounding with size/maturity.

---CRITIQUE Rich Price Funding Illiquid Asset Build---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 2
RATIONALE: The quality leg is growth in non-current assets, which is essentially the published asset-growth anomaly (Cooper–Gulen–Schill) whose documented concentration among richly priced firms makes the interaction a rediscovery rather than a new mechanism, and GROWTH on a base that can be near zero adds instability.

---CRITIQUE Liquid Assets To Price With Light Obligations---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 2
RATIONALE: The stated hypothesis is a diagnostic decomposition ("which component drives the alpha") rather than an economic mechanism, and the resulting construct is simply cheap-on-current-assets times low-leverage — a standard and much-studied value×leverage tilt that closely overlaps the archived ceq/mktcap × act/at signal.

---CRITIQUE Liquid Claim Tested Through The Cycle---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 3
RATIONALE: The through-cycle minimum is a legitimately novel durability concept, but TS_MIN((act−lt)/at,5) is highly correlated with the current (act−lt) that already forms the numerator of the valuation leg, so the product is closer to squaring one balance-sheet quantity than to gating value on an independent quality dimension.

---SIGNAL 1---
NAME: Rank-Weighted Stock And Flow Claim Cheapness
EXPRESSION: MUL(IND_RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(MA(ADD(ib, dp), 3), MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 3)))
HYPOTHESIS: The shareholder's claim is both a stock of unencumbered liquid assets and a recurring stream of cash earnings, and neither should dominate the other by an accident of accounting magnitude; a firm cheap on both components at once, while earning gross profit, is the strongest quality-value case.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite
REASONING: Combining the two claim components as equally weighted ranks removes the implicit one-times capitalization of the flow term that made the earlier additive version numerically indistinguishable from its balance-sheet leg, so the flow genuinely moves the ordering. This makes the test meaningful: if it beats the archived net-liquid-claim signal, the recurring-cash component adds information the stock claim misses, which is exactly the question the archive leaves open.
REASONING_END

---SIGNAL 2---
NAME: Liquid Claim With Pricing Power
EXPRESSION: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), revt), 3)))
HYPOTHESIS: A discounted, liquid firm is a quality-value case when it sells at a genuine markup over its own input costs, because pricing power is what allows the business to keep generating the liquidity behind the discount; a commodity business with no margin has nothing but its liquidation value and will consume it.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional
REASONING: Gross margin per dollar of sales is a pure income-statement measure of competitive position that contains no balance-sheet quantity, so unlike profit-scaled-by-liabilities it is not mechanically correlated with the valuation leg and cannot degenerate into a low-leverage screen. It is also economically different from the archived gross-profits-to-assets leg, which mixes margin with asset turnover, so a result would tell us which of the two components of profitability the trap distinction actually needs.
REASONING_END

---SIGNAL 3---
NAME: Rich Price With Swelling Operating Assets
EXPRESSION: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), IND_RANK(DELTA(RATIO(act, revt), 1)))
HYPOTHESIS: When a richly priced firm's receivables and inventory rise relative to the sales they are supposed to support, revenue is being pulled forward or goods are not selling, and the high valuation rests on a working-capital build that must unwind; such firms should underperform.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional
REASONING: The quality leg is the change in days of working capital carried per dollar of sales, an operating-efficiency deterioration measure, not growth in the long-lived asset base, so it is distinct from the asset-growth anomaly and is scaled by revenue rather than by a near-zero base. Pairing it with an expensiveness-oriented valuation leg keeps the cross-sectional slope and the portfolio alpha pointing the same way, which is where all previous short-side attempts broke down.
REASONING_END

---SIGNAL 4---
NAME: Cheapness With Operating Cash Runway
EXPRESSION: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(che, cogs)))
HYPOTHESIS: A cheap firm realises its value only if it can wait; cash measured against the annual cost of running the business is the firm's survival horizon, and a firm with several quarters of costs in hand never has to issue equity at a depressed price, whereas a firm with weeks of runway must dilute its owners exactly when the discount is widest.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional
REASONING: Cash scaled by operating costs is a survival-horizon concept rather than a leverage or asset-composition ratio, so it is economically distinct from the liability-intensity and current-asset-share screens the archive has already tested, and it explains *why* liquidity matters for value realisation rather than merely restating that it does. Both inputs are near-universally reported, keeping coverage in the high tier, and the interaction targets the specific mechanism — forced dilution at depressed prices — that converts cheapness into a trap.
REASONING_END

---SIGNAL 5---
NAME: Liquid Claim With Trough Profitability
EXPRESSION: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(TS_MIN(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 5)))
HYPOTHESIS: What separates a quality-value firm from a trap is not its average profitability but its worst year: a cheap, liquid firm that stayed profitable through its own five-year trough has a business that does not break, while one whose current profitability sits above a deeply negative trough is cyclically flattered.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional
REASONING: Moving the through-cycle minimum from the balance-sheet claim to profitability removes the mechanical correlation with the valuation leg that made the earlier version close to squaring one quantity, while preserving the durability concept the critic judged genuinely novel. It also poses a clean question against the archive, whose profitability screens all use three-year averages: whether the trough or the mean is the informative moment of the quality distribution.
REASONING_END
